messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rangi is a 56-year-old Māori man, divorced, who has worked as a detective for nearly two decades. He presented for assessment with a PCL-5 score of 62, describing a clinical picture that has quietly consumed him for most of his adult life before finally, in recent months, becoming impossible to contain.

The trauma at the centre of Rangi's presentation is not a single incident but a sustained architecture of violence. Throughout his childhood, his primary caregiver — a man he describes only as "the old man" — subjected him to systematic physical abuse that was unpredictable in its timing but consistent in its cruelty. What Rangi remembers most viscerally is the smell: burnt food, singed fabric, the acrid haze that preceded the worst episodes, when the old man's rage would find its focus on him. He remembers believing, even then, that there was something about him that invited it — that he was, in some essential way, the kind of boy this happened to. That belief did not leave him when he grew up. It calcified.

For years, Rangi managed. He entered law enforcement, drawn perhaps by a need to impose order on the chaotic, and rose to detective. But the work placed him in proximity to the very material his mind had never processed. On scene visits, interviewing victims, reviewing case files — he encountered people whose faces, whose body language, whose visible suffering mirrored something he had never let himself fully name. When he saw a victim who resembled the children he had once been, or walked into a space where something had been burning, the full memory returned without transition or warning — not as recollection but as reinstatement, as if fifty years had not passed. He would feel it in his body first: his chest tightening, his jaw locking, a surge of physical reactivity so intense that colleagues had twice asked if he was having a cardiac event. He told them he was fine.

The rage that accompanied these returns was something Rangi found almost more distressing than the fear. When the memories came, they brought with them a fury so consuming he could not finish sentences — he would lose the thread of what he was trying to explain and go silent, which he read as further evidence that he was broken, that his reactions since the event proved he was a lousy coper who had never managed to become someone capable of handling his own history. This self-condemnation deepened the memories' grip: the more he believed the abuse had happened because of who he was, the more the memories returned saturated with shame and rage, and the more those memories confirmed, in his mind, that his beliefs about how the world works — that people can be safe, that suffering is not deserved — had been permanently destroyed.

To manage, Rangi built a careful life of avoidance. He stopped wearing certain colours and cuts of clothing that resembled what he had worn as a child, a habit so automatic he could no longer fully explain it. He withdrew from colleagues socially, declining invitations, eating alone, gradually becoming someone his team described as "private." He learned to detach himself from the memories when they surfaced — to observe them from a remove, as if watching footage of someone else — believing this was control. But detachment kept the memories unprocessed and structurally intact, so that the next trigger — a burnt smell drifting from the break room at the precinct, a victim's face in a photograph — could instantly reinstate the full experience again. The avoidance, which was meant to reduce exposure to triggers, had instead preserved the sensitivity to them; and the social withdrawal had removed the relationships that might have offered any corrective experience, leaving him only with the conclusion that he was someone others were right to keep at a distance.

At night, Rangi could not surrender to sleep. He lay alert, monitoring, certain that lowering his guard was a risk he could not afford — a vigilance that had protected a child and now exhausted a man. Positive emotions, when they arose, confused and unsettled him; he had no framework for them, and their presence felt wrong in a way he could not articulate.

What finally brought him in was a case he could not close — not professionally, but internally. He had interviewed a child victim three months ago and had not slept properly since. He came to the intake session hoping, he said quietly, to find out whether any of this could be different. What he feared most was that it could not.
